title: 1.5 · Build a block (Functions, decomposition, remix)
name: Build a block (Functions, decomposition, remix)
summary: Students name a group of steps once and use it everywhere: a My Block. In Robo Route they call a ready-made block for every stair, split a route into named legs, and remix blocks from the Starter shelf, changing one step and keeping the line that says where the block came from. Pairs share one device.
iCan: break a big route into named parts
make a My Block once and call it many times
remix a block someone else made, change it, and keep the credit
materials: Dance Blocks printable (move cards, a block name card, a based-on tag)
doNow: Name three things that getting ready for school is made of. Which one could you give a one-word name?
plan: Explore: call the Stair block, open it, name it

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 1.4, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 1.4

do: Open Robo Route at Functions on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Level 1 is a staircase of three stairs, and a block named Stair is already made. Read the learn card, then tap call three times and run it. Open the Stair block to show the five steps inside it.

Open level 4 to show the Starter blocks shelf: blocks other people made, each with a line that says where it came from. Open Zig, add one forward at the start, and point at the credit line that stays on.
say: Name a group of steps once, use it everywhere. A My Block is a group of steps with a name; a call block runs the whole group wherever you put it.
You may change a block someone else made: that is a remix. Keep the line that says where it came from, so everyone knows who started it.
ask: What would you name this block so a friend understands it?
explore.afterAsk: Collect three names for the Stair block and three for a block that crosses a room. Keep the ones that say what the block does, not who made it or how long it is.
explore.bigIdea: Name a group of steps once and use it everywhere; when you change someone else's block, keep the credit.

play.goal: 4 levels, so everyone remixes a starter block
play.stretch: the chapter, then 3 stars; level 6 is three named legs
play.pairs: driver and navigator on one device; the Swap! banner shows every 3 levels; the navigator names the block out loud before the driver makes or calls it
lookFors: defining a block and never calling it: Run stays dimmed until a call exists and the hint says why
deleting the credit line on a remixed block, or changing nothing and calling it a remix
on levels 3 and 6, one giant block with every step instead of one block per leg
play.misconception: Making a My Block does nothing by itself: the steps only run when a call block is placed, and a remix keeps the line that says where the block came from.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Which part of your program deserved a name? Why that one?
On level 4 you changed a block someone else made. What did you change, what did you keep, and why does the based on line matter?
showMe: One pair shows level 6 on the projector: the three legs as three named blocks, then the main program with only three calls.

exit.sentencePrompt: How did you split a route into named parts today, and what did you change and keep when you remixed a starter block?
exit.frame: I split ___ into ___ and ___. When I remixed ___, I changed ___ and kept ___.

rubric.line: Decomposing: splitting a route into named parts
levels: Names one part or one block
Names the parts the route was split into and the block made for each
Also says why those parts: they repeat, or each one is easy to check on its own

rubric.line: Remixing: changing a starter block and keeping the credit
levels: Says a block was changed, with no detail
Says which starter block was changed, what changed, and that the based on line stayed
Also says why the change fit the level, or how the remixed block could be used again somewhere else

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: levels 1 and 2 pre-define the block; the pair only calls it
hint 1 names the parts of the route; read-aloud on
the navigator names the block out loud before the driver builds it
stretch: level 6 at par, then rename the three legs so a new player understands them
invent one block that solves two different levels and say what would need to change

unpluggedTwin.title: Dance Blocks
materials: move cards (step, clap, spin, hop, freeze)
one block name card per group
steps: Each group invents a four-move dance from the move cards and gives it a one-word name on the name card. Practice it once.
The class is the program: the caller calls block names (Spin! Wave!) and every group that owns that name does its whole dance. Call the same name twice in a row: one name, many runs.
Remix round: each group swaps dances with another group, changes exactly one move, and clips the based-on tag to the new name card. Perform both versions.
Share: which move did you change and why? What does the based-on tag tell the audience?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: name three things that getting ready for school is made of, and circle the one you could give a one-word name.

Play Robo Route, chapter Functions, in pairs for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 5 1 0 0. Goal: 4 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; sign in with the login cards so the work is saved (signed out is fine only if the cards are missing). No devices or no internet? Run the unplugged twin printed below (Dance Blocks, 15 minutes), then talk about the two discussion questions for 5 minutes.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Which part of your program deserved a name? Why that one?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut; in 5 minutes of Explore do level 1 only and let level 4's learn card teach the remix

add: the Dance Blocks twin (15 minutes) before Play
the 3-star stretch and level 6 after Play
10 minutes of the Unit 1 review on Brain Board

notes: Run stays dimmed while a block is defined but never called; that is the lesson's most useful nudge, so let pairs find it.
Levels 4 and 5 use the Starter blocks shelf: the remix must change a real step and the credit line must stay on, or the level says so.
Shared devices: this is an odd lesson, so partner A signs in; the gradebook and the Standards tab count the signed-in student.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Name three things that getting ready for school is made of. Which one could you give a one-word name?

Big idea: Name a group of steps once and use it everywhere; when you change someone else's block, keep the credit.

We will talk about:
- Which part of your program deserved a name? Why that one?
- You changed a block someone else made. What did you change, what did you keep, and why?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play: Functions
steps.body:
Goal: 4 levels, so you remix a starter block. Stretch: finish the chapter, then 3 stars.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 5 1 0 0.
Pairs: driver and navigator. Swap when the Swap! banner shows. The navigator names the block out loud before the driver makes or calls it.
A My Block only runs when you call it. When you remix a starter block, keep its based on line.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about My Blocks, named parts and remixing.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
How did you split a route into named parts today, and what did you change and keep when you remixed a starter block?
